news.title: What commodity markets can expect from the Trump-Xi summit
news.text:
Trade in agriculture,
energy and rare earths has become major bargaining chips in the
trade war between the United States and China and are ​likely to
feature again when President Donald Trump hosts his counterpart
Xi Jinping in Washington next week.

Here's what ‌else we know:

AGRICULTURE

Agricultural goods, led by soybeans, are one of the biggest
US ​exports to China, reaching $29 billion in 2024. They are also
among the least ⁠sensitive parts of the trade relationship and
thus a likely area for agreement.

At the Busan summit in South Korea last year, China agreed
to purchase 25 million metric tonne of US soybeans annually
through 2028, ‌according to the White House. US officials say
Beijing then agreed to add on another $17 billion in other
agricultural product purchases during Trump's visit to Beijing

Beijing has never acknowledged those agreements, but is
nonetheless on track to meet the ‌soybean ⁠commitment. Hitting the
other will probably require exempting agricultural imports from
a final 10 per cent ⁠tariff leftover from the trade war.

Analysts expect some waivers after US Trade Representative
Jamieson Greer said on September 3 there could be announcements
to incentivise US agricultural sales to China. Sorghum and corn
are candidates as historically they ​were the largest exports
apart from soybeans.

China has ‌been a modest, if intermittent, buyer of US oil
and gas over the past decade, but imports ground to a halt last
year after Beijing imposed tariffs of 10 per cent to 15 per cent. Washington has
been pushing to change that since Trump's visit to Beijing in

Bloomberg ‌reported on Tuesday energy tariffs could be part
of a $30 billion package of ​reciprocal tariff cuts flagged after
the May summit but not yet implemented. That could lead to the
resumption of imports, which annually ranged from $7.5 billion
to $12 ⁠billion between the end of the previous trade war in 2020

However, that would not immediately translate to a big new
windfall for US LNG producers. While Chinese imports of LNG
stopped ‌after the tariffs, Chinese buyers are still fulfilling
long-term contracts with their US suppliers but reselling the
cargoes after purchase.

China has historically been among the largest buyers of
Iranian and Russian crude oil and the US has sanctioned refiners
and other entities for the trade over the years. Ahead of the
summit, the US has raised the possibility of ending some
sanctions while also threatening to impose others.

Trump said he would consider lifting some sanctions after
his visit to ‌Beijing, although they remain in place. Since
August, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has overseen a new
push to ​impose secondary sanctions on banks financing Iranian
trade, although Chinese banks have been conspicuously absent.

RARE EARTHS

China's control over production of rare earths and its
decision to ⁠limit exports to the US brought Trump to the
negotiating table this year, and while more ⁠material is now
flowing from China, the issue is not fully resolved.

US firms in sensitive industries such as aerospace or
chipmaking still struggle for access, while some Chinese
exporters ‌refuse to ship to the US for fear of repercussions
from Beijing if the relationship worsens again.

Reuters has reported that the issue was on the US planning
agenda and ​US officials have repeatedly called on Beijing to
honour its commitments to keep the critical materials flowing.

Published on September 18, 2026

news.title: Age of Redundancy
news.text:
By Stephen Holmes

Few ideas have traveled as far as the Great Replacement, which holds that native populations are being deliberately supplanted by immigrants. Coined in France by the writer Renaud Camus, it has furnished the grammar for the advance of Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, Viktor Orbán’s long reign in Hungary, the Alternative für Deutschland in Germany, and Donald Trump’s mass-deportation program in the United States. It has also been cited by mass murderers in Christchurch, El Paso, Hanau, and Buffalo. The idea’s potency is easy to understand. It converts a diffuse unease about demographic change into a story with heroes, villains, victims, and remedies. It tells believers that they are being pushed aside by identifiable strangers, and that the process can be reversed. It mobilizes voters because it gives fear a face.

That is what makes the current uproar over data centers so strange. Three-quarters of Americans now say they would oppose the construction of a data center in their community: 83% of Democrats, nearly 80% of independents, and two-thirds of Republicans. State legislatures have introduced a growing number of bills to regulate, delay, or block such projects. Governors who courted AI investment have paused new connections to already strained electrical grids. Only Trump still tours the country urging towns to accept what their neighbors are refusing.

How can this bipartisan opposition be explained? At first glance, the two fears resemble one another. Both are about the future. Both involve a sense that one’s place in the country is insecure. Both resonate most in the countryside. And both spring from the conviction that immensely consequential decisions are being made elsewhere, by people who won’t live with the results.

Yet one fear has divided democracies, while the other has united even the most polarized of them. Why should immigration produce rival camps while a large, windowless building generates something close to a national consensus?

One answer is that the objection to data centers is practical. They consume land, water, and immense quantities of electricity. They bring construction work and tax revenue, but few permanent jobs, and their profits flow to distant investors.

A deeper answer lies in what the building says. The factory chimney once told a town something reassuring, even as it poisoned the air: you are needed here. The windowless hall says that only the town’s electricity, water, and land are needed. It says nothing about the people who live there. That silence gives the practical objections their force.

The data center is the visible infrastructure of an economy that seems to need a community’s resources but few of its members. The fear it provokes is not primarily a fear of being replaced. It is the fear of not being worth replacing.

Immigration politics is a politics of competition. This is a politics of redundancy.

The older fear fueled political division because a fear of replacement needs an identifiable replacer. That replacer is a person, and a person has defenders as well as opponents. When one party says that the migrant is taking your place, the other can point to the migrant’s children in the school play and say, “This, too, is the country’s future.” Defenders can add that strangers are needed to fill the jobs natives will not take, and to pay for the pensions natives expect to collect. One person’s rival is another’s neighbor, employee, or child.

Immigration arguments, however bitter, remain arguments about membership in a society that still imagines itself to need human beings. The Great Replacement named an enemy, but it also named a remedy. Deportation flights and a wall are cruel instruments, but they promise reversibility. To fear that strangers will take your job is, at least, to assume that your job will continue to exist. The fear of replacement is the fear of people who still believe they are worth replacing.

Data centers threaten that conviction. They are the most visible infrastructure of an economy that promises, or threatens, to require fewer drivers, clerks, translators, warehouse workers, customer-service representatives, and perhaps eventually professionals.

What sort of social order do such buildings portend? The fear they arouse is not of being outnumbered but of being made useless and unemployable. They foretell an economy in which intelligence is centralized, electricity is consumed on an industrial scale, profits are remote, and the connection between a locality’s contribution and its share of the resulting wealth is obscure.

The new threat has no ethnicity and no passport. Nobody can be rounded up for it. There is only a structure at the edge of town, drawing power for a system that does not seem to require the town at all.

That is why the fear cannot be confined to right-wing populism, and why the populist who made his career on the older fear is helpless before the new one. Trump could tell his voters they were being displaced by their inferiors. He cannot tell them that they are not worth replacing. Nor can he tell them who is doing the replacing, because the men doing it stood beside him at his inauguration.

The base that believed him about the border does not believe him about the building.

Whom do you deport to bring back a world in which you were needed? A rival can be expelled. No such remedy exists for a job that has become obsolete.

For much of American history, immigration was driven not only by war, persecution, and family ties, but by employers’ demands for labor. Farms, factories, railroads, hospitals, and households needed more workers. If demand contracts across a widening range of occupations, Trump’s wall may come to seem unnecessary, not because Americans have settled their quarrel over belonging, but because the economy has become less dependent on newcomers and natives alike.

The backlash against data centers is unsettling the old politics without yet settling into a new one. Its unanimity reflects not a country that has overcome polarization, but a threat that resists being sorted by party. A fear with a face can engender parties, counterparties, and a program of expulsion. A fear without a face produces moratoria.

Today’s cross-party protest will hold only until people are asked what future they want. Is it merely to build the data center somewhere else?

The Great Replacement was a lie that told its believers their place was worth stealing. The building at the edge of town makes no such promise. It is not coming for your place. It has no use for it.

The writer is Professor of Law at New York University School of Law.

news.title: US again denies Pal­estinian President visa to attend UN assembly
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The United States has denied Pal-estinian President Mahmoud Abbas an entry visa to attend the UN General Assembly in New York next week, extending a ban in place since last year, a Pal-estinian official familiar with the matter said on Thursday.

Without naming specific officials, the State Department said on Wednesday it would extend visa sanctions against Palestinian officials over actions they took to “internationalise the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals.

It marks the second year in a row that President Donald Trump’s administration has prevented Abbas from speaking in-person to the gathering of world leaders, where several US allies last year recognised Palestine as a state.

The Palestinian official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, confirmed Abbas’s visa had been denied.

Palestinian Authority warns decision could hinder two-state solution

In a statement, the Palestinian Authority’s foreign ministry described the measure as counter to “developing Palestinian-US relations and creating the political climate necessary to implement the two-state solution and achieve peace and stability in the region”.

The ministry also “expressed its astonishment at the US statement’s disregard for the substantive reforms carried out by the State of Palestine”. It said these included reforms to the social welfare system, as well as those in the financial, administrative, educational, and legal fields “according to clear, transparent, and verifiable mechanisms”.

Palestinian officials say that decades of US-mediated talks have failed to end Israeli occupation and secure an independent Palestinian state.

Under a 1947 UN “headquarters agreement”, the US is generally required to allow access for foreign diplomats to the UN in New York. However, Washington has said it can deny visas for security, extremism and foreign policy reasons.

President Trump’s policies have regularly targeted Palestinians, pro-Palestinian voices and critics of US ally Israel. Internationally, the Trump administration has sanctioned International Criminal Court officials, including prosecutors and judges. The court’s decision to issue an arrest warrant in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity during Israel’s assault on Gaza has drawn Washington’s ire.

Domestically, the Trump administration has attempted to deport pro-Palestinian foreign protesters, threatened a funding freeze for universities over protests and enforced social media screening for immigrants.

news.title: A sweeping US sanctions bill offers Ukraine new leverage on Russia
news.text:
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine has long argued that Russia will only negotiate seriously if the cost of continuing the war becomes too high.

For Kyiv, punitive sanctions that impose real economic costs on Moscow are a key part of that strategy.

This week’s passage of a long-sought, sweeping package of U.S. sanctions aimed at cutting off some of the financial resources President Vladimir Putin relies on to fund the war gives Ukraine another potential source of leverage, but its impact may depend on whether and how aggressively the measures are implemented by the United States.

The House on Wednesday approved the sanctions package targeting Russian officials and key sectors of the economy. On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the vote “symbolic,” adding that the House passed the bill on the same night Russia launched another large-scale attack across Ukraine, capabilities the full implementation of the deal would derail. 

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that if the United States imposes additional sanctions on Russia, it would hinder the Washington-led effort to end the war in Ukraine.

“We are, of course, monitoring the passing of this document. This falls into the category of unfriendly actions. And, of course, the U.S. imposing some additional sanctions would definitely complicate the efforts to find a peace settlement in Ukraine,” Peskov told reporters during his daily conference call.

“For Ukraine, the immediate benefit is political, not economic. Congress signaling political solidarity with Ukraine via its legislative support sends a valuable message to the Kremlin,” said Tom Keatinge, director of the Centre for Finance and Security at RUSI. 

Here’s why the sanctions package matters to Ukraine:

For Kyiv, the sanctions package offers another, powerful, way to increase economic pressure on Moscow.

Existing Western sanctions have imposed significant costs on Russia, but Kyiv has argued that they have not delivered the swift, severe economic impact needed to force a change in Moscow’s calculations.

“The U.S. House of Representatives’ passage of the Graham bill last night marks an important step toward further pressuring Russia, raising the cost of its continued aggression, and depriving the Russian war machine of resources," said Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha in comments to the press on Thursday. "It is crucial not to stop there. We very much hope that this decisive move will...signal the start of a new round of intensified pressure from other partners as well.”

The new legislation targets Russian officials, financial institutions and the network of tankers used to move Russian oil while evading sanctions. It also gives President Donald Trump the authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, subject to specified exemptions.

The measure passed the Senate 86-11 in August and cleared the House 262-159 on Wednesday, sending it to Trump for his signature.

Kyiv has also sought to bring the costs of the war deeper into Russia through long-range strikes on oil refineries and energy infrastructure. The sanctions add to that military pressure by adding economic repercussions, especially if the sanctions target buyers and networks helping sustain Russian energy. 

Securing that economic pressure has been a central focus of Zelenskyy’s lobbying and diplomatic efforts.

The bill is named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. Helping get it across the finish line was his final legislative effort: Graham spent more than a year negotiating the measure and secured an agreement with the White House shortly before his death.

Graham and Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, along with other supporters of Ukraine, spent more than a year building support for the legislation and negotiating a version that could win backing from both the White House and Congress.

Zelenskyy also intensified his lobbying of U.S. lawmakers, including a closed-door meeting with senators following Graham’s funeral.

He used the meeting to make the case for continued U.S. support, describing Ukraine’s efforts to take the fight to Russia while pressing for sanctions aimed at cutting into the oil and gas revenues financing Moscow’s war effort.

He told lawmakers that the legislation was needed not only to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but also to bolster the morale of Ukrainian troops and civilians.

For Ukraine, the central question now is how aggressively the Trump administration will use the new powers to pressure Moscow.

“Sanctions must be strong so that all efforts for peace, and in particular our joint diplomatic efforts with the United States, Europe, and other friends, are effective,” Zelenskyy said Thursday.

There are caveats. The bill gives the president discretion over how it is implemented, including authority over imposing tariffs and the ability to waive certain sanctions under specified conditions.

“Ultimately, this comes down to Trump’s commitment. He already has the tools to sanction Russia on his desk but has chosen to ignore supporting Ukraine in favor of a belief that his skill as a negotiator can end the war. Perhaps he has finally realized that economic pressure - his preferred response to all disputes - is the right tool in this case too,” said Keatinge. 

That has raised concerns among some lawmakers that the administration could either wield the tariff powers too broadly, potentially affecting U.S. allies, or choose not to enforce the sanctions as aggressively as supporters envision.

Trump has so far favored diplomacy with Moscow, leaving open the question of how aggressively his administration will use the new sanctions powers to pressure Russia.
news.summary: Ukraine believes Russia will only negotiate seriously if the war becomes too costly

news.title: Trump says end to Iran war ‘may be near’
news.text:
US president says Iranian leaders want a deal, claims he has heard directly from Tehran• CDF Munir, Iran FM Araghchi discuss regional developments• Washington allows Iranian leaders to attend UN General Assembly

WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said he hoped an end to the war against Iran was near, as the conflict, now in its seventh month, escalated with Saudi aircraft pounding Yemen and Houthi fighters launching drones and missiles at Saudi cities.

The US president is due to meet Gulf leaders on the margins of the UN General Assembly in New York next Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the conflict, according to a report by Axios.

Hours after news broke of the Houthi-Saudi exchanges, Trump told reporters: “Well, hopefully we are towards the end of the war.”

On Iran, he repeated a familiar refrain: “They want to make a deal. We’ll see how that works out.” He said he had been in direct contact with Tehran, but gave no further details.

There is little sign of an imminent resolution. Trump has repeatedly shifted his stated goals and timelines since the war began on Feb, 28 when US and Israeli forces struck Iran and Tehran retaliated against Israel and Gulf states hosting American bases.

The strikes on Iran, and Israeli attacks on Lebanon, have killed thousands and displaced millions.

Trump has said curbing Iran’s nuclear capability is among his objectives, though Iran maintains it does not possess nuclear weapons and that its uranium enrichment programme is for civilian purposes.

Axios reported that the New York meeting would include representatives from all six Gulf Cooperation Council states: Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman.

The report relied on unnamed sources; the White House and State Department did not respond to requests for comment.

Regional diplomacy continues

Separately, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir discussed the latest regional developments in a phone call during the foreign minister’s visit to Beijing on Wednesday, Iranian media reported, as US-Iran negotiations remain stalled with no agreement in sight.

Meanwhile, China’s foreign minister, Wang Yi, told the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, in a call on Thursday that the two countries “should prepare well for the next stage of high-level interactions in the spirit of equality, respect and reciprocity”, according to a ministry statement, which described head-of-state diplomacy as the “anchor” of the relationship.

The statement stopped short of confirming a meeting between Xi Jinping and Trump, which Trump has said would take place on Sept 24 during Xi’s visit to Washington.

Wang and Rubio also discussed the Middle East, a day after Wang hosted Araghchi in Beijing, where he urged Iran and the US to show restraint, return to the interim peace deal signed in June, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration will allow top Iranian officials to attend the United Nations General Assembly in New York next week, the State Department said on Thursday, even as Washington and Tehran remain at war and continue intermittent talks aimed at ending the conflict.

A State Department spokesperson said a “core delegation from the Iranian regime” would be allowed to attend the meeting in line with the United States’ obligations as the world body’s host country.

That means officials including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi will be granted visas, according to a source familiar with the decision.

The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year,” the State Department spokesperson added.

news.title: 'Do I want to annihilate them?' Trump weighs next phase of Iran war
news.text: US President Donald Trump has once again raised the possibility of resuming a large-scale attack on Iran. His repeated warning comes as Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps keeps the Strait of Hormuz heavily in its control and continues to restrict passage to vessels.In an interview with Axios Trump said that he was approaching a critical decision over the next phase of the Iran war, including whether to launch another round of major attacks.“I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not?” Trump said. “It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me.”Trump’s remarks, however, were not a new threat to destroy Iran. He has made similar threats repeatedly since the conflict began, including warnings of attacks on Iran’s power infrastructure and other vital facilities. Axios described Thursday’s comments as coming at a critical juncture over whether Washington should restart massive attacks.Hormuz remains a flashpointIran has continued to restrict passage through the Strait of Hormuz, while the US has been trying to increase tanker traffic through the waterway and restore the flow of oil to global markets.Coinciding with Trump’s interview, the IRGC Navy also claimed to have struck a Togo-flagged tanker, stating that it was brought to a halt after what they described as an “illegal passage” through the strait. It accused the US military of having “incited and deceived” the vessel into attempting the crossing.The number of commercial vessels crossing the strait has fallen sharply. With incidents like this only leading to more concerns.The US military has also been maintaining a naval blockade on Iranian ports and has attempted to increase tanker movements through Hormuz. Trump told Axios that the blockade had prevented Iran from exporting its oil, saying ships attempting to do so had been attacked.The latest confrontation also comes against a wider deterioration in the region. Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen exchanged fresh strikes, raising concerns about both the Red Sea route and Gulf energy infrastructure.Trump weighs next phase of warTrump said he was considering whether to return to major combat operations against Iran after holding back from doing so earlier this year.According to Axios, Trump had paused plans to resume large-scale attacks in August after Saudi Arabia and Qatar raised concerns that Iran could retaliate against Saudi oil and gas facilities.Since then, Washington has suspended negotiations with Tehran, expanded its sanctions campaign and maintained the naval blockade while focusing military efforts on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.US officials told Axios that Trump and defence secretary Pete Hegseth have ordered US forces in the Middle East to remain at their current levels through the end of the year, keeping Washington prepared for a possible return to full-scale combat.Trump is also expected to meet leaders from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly next week. He said he wanted to hear directly from the Gulf leaders about the war and its next phase.The latest tanker strike therefore comes at a critical moment for the conflict: Hormuz remains heavily restricted, attempts to restore commercial shipping have faced Iranian resistance, and Trump is weighing whether to escalate the war again or pursue a deal.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. The US military maintains a naval blockade on Iranian ports.  Recent tanker incidents raise concerns about regional stability and oil flow.  Trump will meet Gulf leaders to discuss the conflict's next phase.

news.title: FA chief asks Infantino to release records on World Cup plan
news.text:
LONDON: England FA chair and FIFA vice-president Debbie Hewitt has written to FIFA president Gianni Infantino seeking the release of material related to his abandoned World Cup investment plan and the lifting of US striker Folarin Balogun’s suspension, an FA source confirmed to Reuters on Thursday.

Infantino, 56, has been under mounting pressure since unveiling a proposal to sell a commercial stake in the World Cup to private investors. The plan sparked fierce opposition, with UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and North America’s CONCACAF among those calling for changes at the top of FIFA.

Balogun was handed a one-match ban at the 2026 World Cup after receiving a red card in his side’s 2-0 round-of-32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina that would have ruled him out of their last-16 clash with Belgium.

That prompted US President Donald Trump to contact Infantino and urge him to have the punishment reviewed, with the governing body suspending the ban for one year. The next FIFA Council meeting is scheduled for Oct 15.

The Times reported that Hewitt sent the letter this week to Infantino and FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, calling for an independent review of the selloff plan.

On Wednesday, UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister said the Euro-pean football body remains on course to find a credible challenger to Infan-tino and has not allowed its campaign for change to dissolve into wishful thinking.

McAllister said the candidate for next March’s election need not be European but must be capable of defeating Infantino, uniting football’s confederations and delivering lasting governance reform.

Speaking to Reuters at the World Football Summit in Madrid after UEFA’s Executive Committee met in Thessaloniki, she rejected suggestions that opposition to Infantino had lost momentum despite the FIFA president appearing to retain enough support to win another term.

UEFA’s efforts were not about installing a European figurehead to lead a rebellion, she said, but building support for a candidate with a clear reform programme.

“I don’t think so,” McAllister said when asked whether Infantino’s opponents had overestimated the damage to his authority. “We always knew that things wouldn’t just change overnight. That would be naive. We knew that there would be a resistance to change as well, of course.

“We’re taking things step by step, both legally in terms of the political context with an alternative candidate and in terms of the programme of governance reforms that we need to see.”

news.title: Stocks stage partial recovery on select buying
news.text:
KARACHI: The Pakis-tan Stock Exchange (PSX) on Thursday attracted renewed buying interest in select sectors, helping the benchmark KSE-100 index partially recover overnight losses, despite persistent uncertainty on the economic front due to geopolitical concerns amid elevated crude oil prices.

Topline Securities Ltd said the index rebounded, gaining 1,021.40 points, or 0.67 per cent, to close at 169,043.20, partially recovering from the previous session’s sharp decline. The benchmark traded between 168,223 and 169,577, reflecting elevated volatility despite the positive close.

The recovery was supported by selective buying in key index-heavy stocks after the recent correction. However, market sentiment remained cautious amid ongoing focus on global oil prices, geopolitical developments, domestic macroeconomic indicators, and institutional flows.

Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Ltd (AHL), said investor sentiment improved after US President Donald Trump’s remarks suggesting the war with Iran could be nearing an end, with easing oil prices further supporting sentiment. Reports of additional Saudi crude cargoes being routed through Oman helped ease concerns about potential supply disruptions.

On the corporate front, N-ational Bank informed the PSX that the Federal Constitutional Court of Pakistan announced its judgment on Wednesday (Sept 16) on pensioners’ entitlement to government-announced pension increases and dismissed the bank’s appeal.

On the index contribution front, Pakistan Petroleum, United Bank, Mari Energies, Bank Alfalah, Habib Bank, Engro Holdings, Lucky Cement, Oil and Gas Development Company, Meezan Bank, and Maple Leaf Cement Factory were the top positive contributors, collectively adding 717 points to the index.

Market activity remained relatively stable, with trading volume edging up 8.48pc to 386.3 million shares and the traded value rising 3.10pc to Rs20.09bn. Media Times Ltd led the volume chart with 42m shares.

Analysts suggest that buying interest may revive if geopolitical tensions ease and oil prices decline. 

Nonetheless, high energy prices, external-sector risks, and the upcoming IMF review will continue to be significant factors shaping market trends.

Published in Dawn, September 18th, 2026

news.text:
Here are Thursday's latest updates:

■ Washington approved a potential $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, including 49 Pratt & Whitney engines, communications equipment, spare parts and other support, the State Department said.

■ Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement said that Saudi-backed forces killed three children and wounded several people in strikes in Taiz province, near the Red Sea port city of Mocha, according to the group's Almasirah television.

■ One person was killed and two wounded in Saudi Arabia by debris from an intercepted Houthi drone, Saudi authorities said. The death was the first announced in the kingdom this month from Houthi attacks.

■ Iranian forces have downed at least two U.S. MQ-1 unmanned aircraft in recent days, U.S. officials told CBS News. At least 24 MQ-9 Reapers and an MQ-4C Triton have also been lost during the war, according to a Congressional Budget Office report.

■ China has privately asked Iran to use its influence over the Houthis to curb their activity, according to Iranian sources, after Saudi Arabia appealed to Beijing for help amid growing threats to shipping and Saudi oil exports.

■ U.S. President Donald Trump told Axios he faces a "big decision" over whether to resume major attacks against Iran, saying he must decide whether to "annihilate" his Iranian foes. Trump also said Iran is in direct contact with the U.S. and wants a deal.

■ Pakistan's defense minister said Islamabad would invoke its defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey following a Houthi drone attack near Mecca, while saying he did not believe Iran would support the Houthis in a way that would open another regional front.

■ The U.S. sanctioned an Iranian cryptocurrency exchange controlled by sanctioned financier Babak Zanjani, accusing it of processing payments for ships seeking safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and routing hundreds of millions of dollars to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

■ The death toll in Gaza since the start of the war has risen to 73,821, with 174,897 people wounded, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing Palestinian medical sources.

news.title: Ireland to acquire long-range radar systems from French military
news.text:
The aim is to improve Ireland’s ability to police its own skies and provide a “complete recognised air picture of Irish airspace".

“Today is a further significant milestone in terms of delivery of the military radar programme, which was a key recommendation made by the Commission on the Defence Forces,” said minister for defence Helen McEntee.

Concerns around Ireland’s ground-based air defence capability have been heightened by multiple high-profile incidents.

During a diplomatic visit from Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy in December, multiple drones were identified in Irish skies. 

Last week, an unidentified drone was spotted by a commercial aircraft flying off the east coast, ahead of the visit of US president Donald Trump.

Drones can often be deployed by foreign states seeking to gather aerial reconnaissance and intelligence on rival powers’ infrastructure and military sites.

The Department of Defence said Ireland’s ground-based air defence capabilities will continue to be beefed up, alongside the development of maritime radar capability.

A recent report from the Wall Street Journal branded Irish waters Nato's “blind spot”, claiming the prevalence of sub-sea cables off Ireland’s coast was prone to Russian sabotage due to Ireland’s defensive frailties.

news.title: Trump tells outdoorsmen at White House dinner he is so powerful he could ban fishing
news.text:
Donald Trump told guests at a Rose Garden dinner for outdoor enthusiasts and industry executives that he is so powerful as president that he could ban them from fishing.

Trump made the quip during the Thursday evening event at the White House, where he signed executive orders aimed at expanding hunting and fishing opportunities and reversing certain Biden-era restrictions.

One of the executives in attendance was Johnny Morris, the billionaire founder of Bass Pro Shops.

Trump told his audience that his executive orders would help expand the fishing season and help those industries participating in the activity.

“That means you can sell a lot of fishing rods, Johnny. You’re going to sell a lot of rods. I could have made it so you couldn’t sell. You couldn’t sell anything. I could have banned fishing,” Trump mused.

“I’ll tell you what. The power of this office is crazy. I could have banned fishing and driven Johnny right the hell out of business. Okay. I think I’m going to do that. Just maybe just a quick order, just for a day or two, till he calls me and he says, ‘Please, President, please, you’re putting me out of business, sir.’”

Trump told the audience that only one other president could rival the former New York City real estate developer for support from America’s hunters and fishermen: “America's outdoorsmen have not had a better friend in the Oval Office for many, many years. Probably the late great President Theodore Roosevelt was very good.”

In typical Trump fashion, the president also boasted to dinner guests about his latest renovation projects around Washington, D.C. 

“We've done a lot of work on the White House,” Trump said in the Rose Garden, which he paved over to make way for a Mar-a-Lago style patio. “The exterior was in bad shape, very, very bad shape.”

Trump specifically mentioned his new black and white granite helipad designed to look like the presidential seal and constructed right on the South Lawn of the White House.

“What they've been able to do with stone, with granite, six inches thick, carved with a beautiful eagle. It's a helipad where the helicopters can land. Never had that before,” the president said. 

“Frankly, the new helicopters that were purchased are so powerful that they ripped the grass out. I said, ‘What about trying to build a helipad,’ and it really came out good, very good.”

At an Oval Office event in July, Trump said that Sikorsky Aircraft, a subsidiary of the mega defense contactor Lockheed Martin, was paying for the helipad because they felt “a little guilty” for not warning about the power of the fleet of helicopters they completed in 2024 for use as the president’s Marine One.

“They are paying for the cost of it – it’s about $5 or $6 million,” Trump told reporters at the time.
news.summary: Trump has boasted about his new helipad constructed right in the backyard of the White House during the event
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Anthropic says its model Claude is helping to build the next version of itself
news.text:
Anthropic's Claude is helping the company develop the next, more intelligent version of the model, the artificial intelligence lab said in an announcement Thursday. 

Claude is leading 26% of Anthropic's model research and development, which the company said means it can complete most of a given task “end-to-end from a high-level prompt" while still being under human supervision. The model is not yet working completely autonomously.

Still, about 90% of the company's research and development is done in “collaboration” with Claude, which Anthropic said means the model can do “large chunks of work under close human direction.”

The announcement came as some leading figures in AI, led in large part by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, are calling for a slowdown in the technology’s development over safety concerns.

As leaders consider pacing AI's development, “we should do everything possible to minimize the gap between what frontier labs know and what the public knows,” the company said in a blog post. “This means better measuring the development of AI, reporting on it publicly, and giving society an opportunity to decide how to use this information.”

The company said that models accelerating their own development could make it “more challenging for humans to understand or control these systems." It argued that sharing these metrics could lead to better understanding of how close leading AI labs are to reaching recursive self-improvement, or a model's ability to autonomously build its successor. 

Anthropic also urged other AI developers to share similar metrics on a regular basis, encouraging the use of a public methodology so the numbers could be compared over time, and potentially across labs. 

It was unclear from Anthropic's disclosure how close the company believes it is to achieving recursive self-improvement, but the pace at which Claude has increasingly contributed to research and development is notable. The portion of work Claude “leads,” or does in large part while remaining under human supervision, was none in February. Six months later, it was leading a quarter of research and development work, reaching that benchmark in August. 

The company also shared details of agent oversight measures it has in place, noting that there were approximately 30,000 agents doing research and engineering work as of August. Oversight measures are crucial for seeing how often agent misbehavior is detected by monitoring systems, the company said. Anthropic recently committed to setting up external third-party evaluators who will be embedded within the company to monitor safety efforts.

An Anthropic researcher kicked off much of the recent dialogue around AI safety when he resigned last week with a dire warning about the threats the technology poses to humanity. Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Elon Musk and other tech leaders have since supported the idea of slowing down development, but other tech leaders and President Donald Trump have pushed back.
news.summary: Anthropic has announced that its AI model, Claude, is significantly aiding in the development of building its successor
news.author: Kaitlyn Huamani

news.title: UAE minister calls datacenters ‘more important than roads’, unveils new ‘hiding rule’
news.text: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) will overhaul its regulatory framework for data centres and halt public disclosure of their physical locations to shield them from military threats, according to comments reported by The Next Web of a session from Salesforce's annual event Dreamforce 2026. Speaking alongside Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff at the Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE’s Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, warned that computing hubs have evolved into critical infrastructure that requires heightened protection.Al Olama said that data centres have become prime targets because our whole lives exist on connected devices, arguing that they are now more important than bridges, roads, or tunnels. In remarks highlighted in the 'The Next Web' report, the minister stated that the UAE will no longer promote the locations of these facilities to prevent bad actors from targeting them, adding that he expects other nations will soon be forced to adopt similar measures. "Unfortunately they’re more important than bridges. They’re more important than roads. They’re more important than tunnels because our whole lives are on these devices that we’re using," said Al Olama, in a session Salesforce published.Incidentally, UAE minister's views are very different from that of most Americans. While Donald Trump government strongly supports data centres, most states across the US are not in strong favour of them. The debate around data center projects is one of the rare modern issues to cut across party lines, demographics and geography -- uniting the US. As a report in AP says, from Republican-dominated Nebraska, Texas and Wyoming to swing-state Pennsylvania to Democratic-leaning New Mexico, in a divided America, the left and right unite to oppose AI data centers.How Iran war changed how UAE deals with data centers 'forever'The strategic shift comes in the wake of severe regional conflict that began on February 28, a day Al Olama recalled preparing for a trip to Ecuador before hostilities escalated. The UAE faced more than 1,000 projectiles and drones during the first week of the conflict alone, with launches from Iran taking only two minutes to reach the country. Al Olama noted that the UAE intercepted more aerial threats than the entire Middle East and Israel combined, resulting in zero impact on human lives or business operations. Domestic life has since returned to normal, though the government is now decentralizing key digital assets, including splitting up its domestic Stargate data centre project and investing in offshore facilities, such as in Germany.Reflecting on broader AI policy, Al Olama warned against allowing fear to choke innovation, drawing a historical parallel to the Middle East’s technological decline after centuries of dominance from 813 to 1515 AD. That era ended when the region banned the Gutenberg printing press for two centuries due to fears over misinformation, alterations to holy scripture, and general administrative anxiety. He cautioned that modern leaders cannot afford to repeat that mistake with artificial intelligence, even if the technology's rapid evolution initially seems frightening.When it comes to public deployment, Al Olama advocated a measured approach that avoids unproven, high-risk systems. UAE public services, such as Abu Dhabi’s TAMM administrative platform, run on established, older large language models rather than cutting-edge frontier systems like OpenAI’s Astra or Anthropic’s Fable, which he warned carry significant cybersecurity and data breach risks. He also drew hard red lines against using AI for predictive policing, citing the danger of false positives, and cautioned against building an oppressive surveillance apparatus, pointing instead to quality-of-life improvements like desk-free biometric airport transit.To insulate the domestic workforce from technological displacement, the UAE has trained all 80,000 federal civil servants in agentic AI, following an earlier initiative that taught prompt design to one million people. Al Olama dismissed fears of mass unemployment, insisting the technology will ultimately create opportunities and boost workforce capability.'One country regulating AI will not work, it has to be almost the entire world'Addressing the global regulatory landscape, Al Olama noted that governments typically overregulate while the private sector tends to underregulate. He pointed to the UAE’s own data protection laws, which were initially drafted by tech companies before state officials and civil society refined them, as a model for collaborative oversight. He warned Western policymakers that unilateral bans on AI would simply hand an insurmountable advantage to competitors, arguing that restrictions in the United States make little sense unless China agrees to follow suit.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.
news.summary: In a bid to bolster data center security, the UAE plans to disguise the physical locations of these critical infrastructures. This strategy is designed to shield them from potential military threats. Furthermore, the nation is diversifying its digital assets and setting up offshore facilities. Minister Al Olama emphasized that excessive caution should not hinder innovation. He also highlighted the necessity of global collaboration for effective artificial intelligence governance.
news.author: TOI TECH DESK

news.title: Iran adds new defenses at deeply buried nuclear site after Trump warns Islamic State not to ‘get cute’
news.text:
New satellite imagery shows Iran has added new defenses around tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain, the deeply buried nuclear-linked site President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike, as Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-drafted Security Council resolution aimed at preserving international monitoring of sanctions on Tehran.

The Institute for Science and International Security said in a report released Thursday that satellite imagery from Sept. 11 shows earthen roadblocks remain in place on roads leading to Pickaxe Mountain’s western tunnel portals near the Natanz nuclear complex. The institute said the continued restricted access reinforces its assessment that the facility is not currently being used for normal operations, while assessing that valuable equipment or materials remain inside.

The report also identified additional soil placed over one western tunnel portal and over a nearby cluster of entrances first built in 2007. The institute said the added soil increases the amount of earth protecting the entrances and helps harden them against aerial bombardment.

The findings come one week after Trump issued his latest warning over Pickaxe Mountain.

“We notice there’s a little activity at Pickaxe,” Trump told reporters last week. “I would advise Iran not to get cute because we will have to hit them very hard.”

Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of attacking the site. In a July 28 “Fox & Friends” interview highlighted by the White House, Trump said the U.S. was watching Pickaxe closely and knew “exactly what’s going on,” adding that Washington could “take out Pickaxe” if diplomacy failed.

Pickaxe Mountain lies roughly two kilometers from Natanz and features multiple tunnel entrances leading into a deeply buried underground complex. Construction began in 2020 following sabotage that damaged an advanced centrifuge assembly facility at Natanz, and Iranian officials subsequently said a replacement underground facility was being built for advanced centrifuge production. Analysts estimate portions of the facility may be buried at least 100 meters beneath the mountain. Iran has said there is no nuclear activity at the site.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital that some analysts believe the opportunity for a straightforward strike on Pickaxe Mountain may already have passed.

“The window to strike Pickaxe Mountain, according to some, has already expired because the regime has dug an underground nuclear facility several times deeper than Fordow,” Ben Taleblu said. But he argued that Washington retains military options even if destroying the underground complex itself proves difficult.

“Washington can do what it’s traditionally been able to do with sites that are underground, hardened and fortified, and that’s to bury their entrances and raise the political cost to the Islamic Republic of being able to dig out,” he said.

“While there may not be the perfect munition just yet, Uncle Sam always has a bigger bomb,” Ben Taleblu added. “And in the meantime, what they can do is show that they mean business by burying the entrances.”

The Pickaxe findings came alongside signs of reconstruction at another sensitive Iranian facility.

In a separate report Thursday, the institute said Iran was “rapidly moving forward” with reconstruction of Taleghan 2 at the Parchin military complex southeast of Tehran. Vantor Technologies satellite imagery from Sept. 13 shows Iran erected a tarp over the destroyed hardened facility, obscuring work underneath from satellite or aerial observation, while dump trucks, bulldozers, concrete equipment and cranes were active around the site.

Follow The Post’s coverage of the war in Iran:

‘Economic D-Day’ sanctions against Iran will be ‘single greatest financial offensive ever’ Bessent says

Iran broadcasts sickening video claiming Barron Trump is ‘fully monitored,’ places $10M bounty on his head

Iran blacklists 45 tankers in Strait of Hormuz, threatens to fine and confiscate cargo

Iran faces massive new triple-threat as Hormuz begins to open, cash gets tight and pols call to end the war

The institute said Iran also built new concrete reinforcement that could provide additional protection against aerial attack. Taleghan 2 was struck by Israel in October 2024 and again in March 2026 after Iran had rebuilt and hardened the facility. The institute said significant questions remain about Tehran’s plans for the site.

The military developments unfolded alongside a separate confrontation over Iran at the United Nations.

Russia and China on Thursday vetoed a U.S.-authored Security Council resolution that would have extended for another year, until September 2027, the mandate of the Panel of Experts supporting the 1737 Iran Sanctions Committee. The measure received 11 votes in favor, while Pakistan and Somalia abstained.

The panel investigates alleged sanctions violations and reports on implementation. The dispute reflects a deeper split over whether UN sanctions suspended under the 2015 nuclear agreement were legally restored through the “snapback” mechanism. Most Council members maintain that the sanctions and related monitoring structures were revived, while Russia and China reject the legal and procedural validity of that position.

A day before the vote, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz told reporters in New York that Washington considers the sanctions legally restored.

“The snapback sanctions… occurred, the United States and this U.N. Security Council followed appropriate procedures for that to occur,” Waltz said Wednesday at a news conference attended by Fox News Digital. “Those sanctions are in place and we expect those who are a party to fully enforce those sanctions.”

Waltz said the expert panel is important because sanctioned companies and individuals can attempt to evade restrictions by changing names and corporate structures.

“The president has been clear, and the world community has been clear with resolution after resolution, that the Iranian regime cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said.

Thursday also brought fresh U.N. scrutiny of both Washington and Tehran. An independent U.N. fact-finding mission said it had reasonable grounds to believe two U.S. strikes on civilian sites in Iran in February constituted war crimes, while separately concluding that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their crackdown on anti-government protests. The mission is investigative rather than judicial, and its findings do not themselves constitute criminal judgments.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Iran U.N. mission for comments but didn’t receive them in time for publication.
news.summary: New satellite imagery reveals Iran has fortified its Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility following military threats from President Donald Trump.
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Judge asked to prevent Trump from carving his name on yet another historic Washington building
news.text:
A federal judge has been asked to prevent President Donald Trump from carving his name on yet another historic building in Washington, D.C.

During his second term, Trump has tried to literally make his mark on Washington, slapping his name on several D.C. landmarks, most notably the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. 

Last December, the State Department announced that it had renamed the U.S. Institute of Peace “to reflect the greatest dealmaker in our nation's history” shortly before Trump hosted a signing ceremony for a peace deal between the presidents of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“Welcome to the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace. The best is yet to come,” the department’s X post read. Trump’s name is tacked onto the building while the “Institute of Peace” is permanently etched in. 

But now, ousted board members of the Institute of Peace asked the court in an emergency motion Thursday to stop any “plans to carve President Trump’s name into the facade of the iconic USIP headquarters building.” The motion was first reported on X by Kyle Cheney, a senior legal affairs reporter for Politico.

“The building — which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation — is a work of expressive architecture designed to be ‘symbolic of USIP’s’ independent ‘mission,’” the emergency motion said, according to a subsequent Politico article. “Alteration of the design to impose a different message would cause irreparable harm.”

Despite Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling Trump the “president of peace” when the building was renamed, the leader of the free world was the one who gutted the think tank created to resolve global conflict. 

Trump called for the dismantling of the Institute of Peace in a February 2025 executive order as part of his and tech billionaire Elon Musk’s effort to reduce what they saw as government waste. 

The executive order led to mass firings at the agency, which are still being challenged in court. 

Most Americans oppose Trump naming government buildings after himself while in office. 

Only 9 percent of Americans said it would be acceptable for Trump to name government buildings after himself while serving as president, according to a Pew Research Center poll released in May. 

Around 70 percent said it would not be acceptable or would only be acceptable after he's no longer leading the country.

Last December, the Trump-appointed Kennedy Center board voted to put the president’s name on the building, prompting a wave of artists to refuse to perform at the arts center. 

In May, U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name to be removed from the Kennedy Center, stating, “Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it.” Weeks later, construction crews were seen taking Trump’s name off the building.
news.summary: Most Americans oppose Trump naming buildings after himself while still in office
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Preparing to leave office, with world beset by problems, UN chief talks of a way forward
news.text:
The world is deeply divided and the U.N.’s most powerful body is paralyzed when it comes to ending conflicts. But there’s a way forward. So says the United Nations’ top official.

On his way out of office at year's end after nearly a decade, U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres — known for doom-and-gloom speeches about the state of the planet — said Thursday he finds hope and possibility in the coming years. But that, he says, is only if the world’s governments can finally cooperate on curtailing conflict, upending inequality and grappling with the arriving juggernaut of artificial intelligence.

“I believe in a number of fundamental things that need to be done, and need to happen for the world to be better — and I’m determined to fight to make those things happen,” Guterres told The Associated Press in a sit-down interview four days before world leaders convene for their annual meeting at the U.N. General Assembly.

His message to leaders and ministers from the U.N.’s 193 member nations coming to U.N. headquarters was no-nonsense: You need to very seriously analyze the fact that the world is facing at least three existential problems -- runaway artificial intelligence, galloping climate change, and escalating inequality that is becoming a serious driver of instability and conflict.

Guterres also warned that the “huge geopolitical divide” and paralysis in the Security Council have created an environment of impunity with powerful countries flouting international law and the U.N. Charter. The invasion of Ukraine by Russia and the attacks on Iran by the United States, both veto-wielding council members, are examples.

“Many countries say, ‘If superpowers can violate the law, why can’t we?’” the secretary-general said. “And so what we are seeing around the world is more and more situations in which countries simply do not care. They do whatever they want, knowing that there will be total impunity.”

 Behavior by nations, he says, is adding fuel to the fire 

The violations and impunity have caused death and enormous destruction, he said, and the combination of the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the broader Middle East conflict are having “a dramatic impact” on the world economy. Food and energy prices are going up, interest rates are rising and developing countries face enormous difficulties in responding to the needs of their people.

He expressed hope that these problems will force people to realize that the obstacles can’t be eliminated alone and require international cooperation. 

That's especially true, he said, with reforms of the institutions formed by the victorious World War II powers — the U.N., especially the Security Council, and the major global financial institutions, the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. They must be overhauled to reflect the realities of the 21st century world where there are emerging economies and powers, he said, and their importance must be reflected in global institutions.

As U.N. chief, the secretary-general has no army, no intelligence service and not much money. But, Guterres said, he has two powers — to speak out on global issues and to convene the world’s nations.

Because of geopolitical divides, Guterres said the United Nations has “no leverage” on promoting peace in Ukraine and the Middle East. But he said he has been firm in defending the U.N. Charter and the territorial integrity of countries, and in condemning “horrible violations of human rights.”

He condemned Hamas’ “intolerable” attack in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and he also condemned “the horrible situation that Israel has created in Gaza with levels of death and destruction that have no parallel in the history of the United Nations.”

The United Nations is not “in a transactional approach to politics,” he stressed. It must be “a reference of values and principles for the whole world, because someone must affirm that the law of force cannot prevail over the force of law.”

“That, of course, sometimes limits our capacity to negotiate an agreement because one of the sides is a clear violator that doesn’t like to listen to the truth. But that will never, never make us move away from what are the values in which a civilized society must be based,” the U.N. chief said.

 He says the AI revolution is sure to loom over this year's UNGA leaders' meeting 

This year’s global gathering is also certain to spotlight the future of the U.N. and the threat of AI getting out of human control.

Guterres has called for international cooperation and guardrails for AI, which he called “a universal problem.” To deal with the escalating problem, he said, countries developing AI at “a higher capacity” should exchange information, establish mechanisms for transparency, have some guardrails and “help create what ideally would be a multilateral mechanism to guarantee that risks can be avoided.”

As for the United Nations., it has serious financial issues, largely due to the U.S. failure to pay billions of dollars to its regular operating budget and the separate budget for the U.N.’s far-flung peacekeeping operations. But it has avoided a financial meltdown and is in the throes of major reforms, which the Trump administration has pressed for.

Even with less resources, Guterres said, the U.N. has been able to maintain its activities, “and I think we demonstrated that we have the best control of public expenditure in any organization of any country in the world.”

Guterres has dealt with U.S. President Donald Trump for nearly six of his 10 years at the helm of the U.N., and he stressed the importance of the U.S.-U.N. relationship, which he said has sometimes been difficult, sometimes easier. Now, he said, the U.N. is cooperating with the U.S. on peace negotiations in the Western Sahara and other parts of the world.

When he meets Trump on Tuesday, the opening day of the global gathering, Guterres said he plans to raise peace in Ukraine and the Middle East, “and I hope that these two objectives might be able to unite the efforts of not only the U.S. and the U.N. but the whole of the international community.” 

Edith M. Lederer has covered international affairs for The Associated Press for more than a half century.
news.summary: The United Nations’ top official acknowledges the world is deeply divided and the U.N.’s most powerful body is paralyzed when it comes to ending conflicts
news.author: Edith M. Lederer

news.title: Is NATO ready to fight? The Ukraine war is raising doubts among military analysts
news.text: Kyiv - Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands of people. It has also served as a proving ground for new weapons systems and raised an uncomfortable question for NATO: Is the alliance prepared for the next war it might have to fight?Five Ukrainian and Western defense officials said developments on the battlefield are moving so quickly that some NATO weapons and tactics risk becoming outdated. While Ukraine — which is not an alliance member — adapts in weeks, NATO buys and develops systems over years, sometimes decades.The Ukraine war and U.S. President Donald Trump’s haranguing of European allies have prompted many NATO members to dramatically increase their defense spending. The Pentagon is currently reviewing its military presence in European countries, which Trump has accused of sponging off U.S. protection and refusing to help prosecute his unpopular war against Iran.
news.summary: Ukrainian and Western defense officials said developments on the battlefield are moving so fast, some NATO weapons and tactics could become outdated.

news.title: Trump signs orders to widen hunting, fishing
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 18 (IANS) US President Donald Trump said he had signed two executive orders to expand hunting and fishing access on federal land and ease restrictions on recreational boating, presenting the measures as victories for outdoor enthusiasts at a White House dinner. Addressing hunters, anglers and outdoor industry leaders in the Rose Garden on September 17, Trump said the orders would also protect traditional lead ammunition and expand fishing seasons and quotas. “With the first order, we're opening up millions of acres of federal land for our hunters and fishers,” he said. Trump said the measure built on actions in August that opened 92 million acres of federal land across 32 states. He did not give a separate acreage figure for the new order. “We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public and hunters, fishers and outdoorsmen should be able to access them. And they weren't able to.” He held up the signed orders during his remarks. Their full texts were not included in the material supplied for this report, leaving the scope and implementation details unclear. Trump said the first order protected the use of lead ammunition, acknowledging that he had needed an explanation of the issue. “So the order protects the use of affordable traditional lead ammunition. That sounds good to me,” he said. Turning to coastal recreation, Trump said the second order removed federal regulations affecting saltwater anglers, boaters, charter captains and coastal communities. He criticised what he described as a Biden administration effort to impose a boating speed limit of 10 miles per hour. He said his administration was eliminating those restrictions immediately. “This order also expands fishing seasons and fishing quotas, undoing another Biden disaster.” Trump did not identify the fisheries covered by those changes or provide revised quotas. He also said his administration had approved all state permits for the 2026 red snapper season ahead of schedule. The president linked the announcements to his support for gun owners and the Second Amendment. He accused former President Joe Biden of waging a “war on gun owners” and cited actions he said had reversed restrictions on firearms dealers and restored veterans’ gun rights. news.title: US Congress passes sweeping Russia sanctions bill
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US lawmakers approved broad new sanctions on Wednesday designed to squeeze Russia over its war in Ukraine, sending the legislation to President Donald Trump after months of delay.

The Republican-led House of Representatives passed the package by 262-159, giving a final congressional green light to the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to office.

Trump has said he will sign the measure, which sailed through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.

The legislation targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions.

It also gives Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas — including potentially China and India — in an effort to choke off revenue financing Moscow’s war.

But its sweeping tariff powers produced an unusual split among Democrats, who overwhelmingly support Ukraine but have resisted handing Trump greater authority over trade.

Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, called the bill “deeply flawed.”

“White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximize President Trump’s authority to impose new import taxes on the American people, and to minimize any obligation to actually impose new sanctions on Russia or its enablers,” he said.

news.title: Taoiseach Micheál Martin to meet UK prime minister Andy Burnham in Manchester today
news.text:
The Taoiseach is the first international leader to be received at No 10 North, with the invite sent by Mr Burham in July.

There will be a private tete-a-tete between Mr Martin and Mr Burnham before a wider meeting with officials present.

The meeting also takes place in the wake of US president Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland last weekend, where he expressed his support for a united Ireland.

It also comes after a meeting between the leaders of Sinn Féin, the Scottish National Party, and Plaid Cymru, which called on the British government to prepare for constitutional change.

Mr Martin had previously said the criteria for calling a border poll was an issue which needed “to be discussed”, given that it is within the purview of the British government to decide when one takes place.

The Good Friday Agreement

“Clearly, at the time of the Good Friday Agreement, that issue [a border poll] was left perhaps deliberately vague," he said. "That’s an issue that, at some stage, needs to be discussed.” 

Mr Burnham also faced significant criticism for his remarks that a border poll was off the table, during a visit to Belfast last month. The criticism lead to Mr Burham subsequently walking back his remarks.

Alongside the visit to No 10 North, Mr Martin and Mr Burnham are due to travel to Wigan for meetings with the Irish community there.

Ahead of his arrival, Mr Martin said he was looking forward to the meeting and to “reaffirming the strength and importance of the relationship between our two countries”.

He said discussions would include Northern Ireland, particularly addressing issues around legacy issues. 

Mr Martin said it was important that progress is made for the “sake of victims and survivors” and for wider reconciliation across the two islands.

“We will also discuss how best to work in partnership to sustain the overall success of the Good Friday Agreement in all its parts in the time ahead,” Mr Martin said.

news.title: US lawmakers urge Trump to press China on detained Americans, AI chips ahead of Xi meeting
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 18 (IANS) US lawmakers have urged President Donald Trump to secure the release of Americans detained in China and restrict Beijing’s access to advanced artificial intelligence chips ahead of his scheduled meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week. The separate demands came as Representative Ro Khanna announced a hearing on a proposed US-China AI safety agreement. His office said the September 23 hearing would take place a day before the leaders’ scheduled White House meeting. On September 17, Senators Edward Markey and Ted Budd introduced a bipartisan resolution condemning what they described as China’s repeated arbitrary or wrongful detention of American academics. Senators John Curtis and Adam Schiff joined the measure. Representatives Stephen Lynch and John Moolenaar led a companion resolution in the House. The lawmakers sought priority for the safe return of Massachusetts academic Youlin Chen and American scholar Min Zin. “President Trump must use his upcoming meeting with President Xi to demand that China release every unlawfully detained American,” Lynch said. The Senate resolution urges the secretary of state to use all available tools to negotiate their release. It calls for raising the China travel advisory from Level 2 to Level 3, which advises Americans to reconsider travel. It also proposes considering a wrongful-detention indicator in the advisory and reviewing the criteria for designating a country as a state sponsor of wrongful detention. The measure supports Trump’s efforts to raise the two cases with Beijing. Separately, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer urged Trump to block China’s access to America’s most advanced AI chips and manufacturing equipment. “Before Trump meets with Xi Jinping next week, he needs to draw a line in the sand and say that blocking the Chinese Communist Party’s access to our cutting-edge AI technology is non-negotiable,” Schumer said on the Senate floor. He said a bipartisan group had introduced legislation as part of the National Defense Authorization Act to restrict chip sales. He accused Trump of obstructing those efforts. Schumer also argued that restrictions on technology transfers could accompany domestic safeguards against AI risks. Maintaining American leadership and limiting those risks were compatible goals, he said. Khanna, the senior Democrat on the House select committee on China, focused on international cooperation over AI safety. “We urgently need an agreement with China on basic inspections and safety standards,” he said. His virtual hearing will examine risks including loss of human control over AI and systems acting against human intentions. Scheduled witnesses include Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton and retired US Air Force Lt. Gen. Jack Shanahan. Khanna said OpenAI and Anthropic had not committed to testifying despite repeated requests. He also wrote to Chinese companies Moonshot AI, Alibaba and DeepSeek, seeking commitments to a binding agreement with American AI laboratories. His office said such an agreement must be enforceable and verifiable. The supplied statements contained no responses from the White House, the Chinese government or the AI companies. Chen, a US citizen who conducted seismological research with Chinese academics, was arrested on November 5, 2024, according to the resolution. It says he has been held for more than 600 days without trial or family access on espionage charges the sponsors describe as baseless. He was denied a lawyer for the first 434 days. Min Zin, a US citizen heading a Myanmar-focused policy think tank, was detained at Kunming Changshui International Airport on June 3, 2026, according to the resolution. He had been invited to an academic event at a university in Yunnan province.
